newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Jubilant fighters seize part of Tajik capital.
newsitem.headline: Jubilant fighters seize part of Tajik capital.

text.p: Fighting in the Tajik capital Dushanbe died down on Sunday after an armed group seized a northern district from a rival warlord, witnesses said.
This correspondent saw fighters in green bandanas wave assault rifles and make jubilant war-cries as they careered around the district in private cars and on army trucks.
A mangled white pick-up truck hit by a rocket and several burned-out homes testified to Saturday's fighting in the district, centring around a cement factory.

Few civilians braved the streets and bazaars were deserted. "People can't work, people can't go about their business peacefully," said Narzalo Tiloyev, 27, an accountant waiting in vain by the side of the road for transport out of the district.
"It was hard before but now it's even harder".

War and instability in Tajikistan, a mountainous country of 5.7 million, has seen the republic carved up into independent fiefdoms controlled by a bewildering array of maverick armed groups much like those in neighbouring Afghanistan.

The victorious men of Sukhrob Kasimov, an Interior Ministry commander, and those of defeated Yakub Salimov, a senior customs official and former interior minister, are nominally loyal to President Imomali Rakhmonov's shaky government.
They have no link to the former Soviet republic's armed Islamic opposition, which signed a peace accord with the government in June aimed at ending four years of civil war.
The government and the opposition had begun a tentative share-out of power and a truce has held broadly since December.
Fighting erupted on Saturday over the killing of Kasimov's uncle. But Western diplomats said tanks and rockets had been used not just to settle a family feud but in a battle for turf.
"This is mafia writ large," one diplomat said.
Russian news agencies also reported a second day of heavy fighting between another two rival groups in the Fakhrobad Valley about 30 km (20 miles) south of Dushanbe.
The reports of fighting between the presidential guard and a force led by a maverick government commander, Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, could not be independently confirmed.
Khudoyberdyev, who has mutinied twice and is seen as a potential coup-maker, had wanted Kasimov to leave the capital.
But the new fighting threatened anarchy in the tense capital, ringed by parched biscuit-coloured mountains.
"There's been a complete breakdown in law and order," said a Western aid worker. "The government looks very weak," she said.
There has been no word from Rakhmonov and a meeting of his Security Council called for Sunday failed to take place.
He is likely to look to a predominantly Russian force of Commonwealth of Independent States peacekeepers to shore up his fragile grip on power -- though its mandate ran out last month.
Nervous peacekeepers set up a control post a few hundred metres (yards) north of his palace on Sunday. "Don't ask us, we have no idea what's going on," a sweating Russian captain said.
About 20,000 Russian troops are carrying out peacekeeping duties and guarding borders in Tajikistan.
The U.S. embassy has advised all its citizens to stay indoors.
There was no word on casualties, but the International Committee of the Red Cross said on Saturday it had supplied a Dushanbe hospital with medicines to treat 40 injured people.

A Canadian couple, Jack White, 63 and Vicky, 56, had no idea fighting had broken out when they flew in on Sunday to set up a school. "I guess the folks back home might be worried. We might be evacuated as soon as we've got here," he said.
